items.followUp: Explain how cohesion between water molecules helps maintain transpiration pull.

rubric.why: Identifies water loss from the leaf as the event that initiates transpiration pull.
rubric.description: Water evaporates from the moist mesophyll cells and diffuses out through the stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing evaporation or water loss from leaf tissues.

rubric.why: Explains that water loss creates a pulling force transmitted through the xylem.
rubric.description: Water loss creates tension or suction in the xylem, pulling the continuous water column upward from the roots.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking tension or suction in the xylem to upward movement of water.

modelAnswer: Water evaporates from the moist mesophyll cells of leaves and diffuses out through the stomata.
This water loss creates tension (suction) in the xylem, pulling the continuous column of water upward from the roots.

items.followUp: State the rules for writing the scientific name of an organism, using humans as an example.

rubric.why: Defines binomial nomenclature as a two-part naming system.
rubric.description: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-word scientific name consisting of genus and species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the scientific name has two parts and identifying them as genus and species.

rubric.why: Checks the order of the two parts of the scientific name.
rubric.description: The genus name is written first, followed by the species name.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the correct order.

rubric.why: Checks the capitalization rule for the genus name.
rubric.description: The genus name begins with a capital letter and the species name begins with a lowercase letter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the correct capitalization of the genus and species names.

rubric.why: Checks the formatting rule for scientific names.
rubric.description: The two words are italicized in print or underlined separately when handwritten.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either accepted formatting convention.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a two-word scientific name: the genus name followed by the species name.
The genus name begins with a capital letter, while the species name begins with a lowercase letter.
Both words are italicized when printed; when handwritten, each word is underlined separately.
For example, the scientific name of humans is *Homo sapiens*.

items.followUp: Name the conducting tissues in plants, give their main components, and state the function of each.

rubric.why: Defines a compound tissue as different cell types working together.
rubric.description: A compound tissue consists of different types of cells that work together to perform a common function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable definition of compound tissue.

rubric.why: Identifies xylem and its transport function.
rubric.description: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to other parts of the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming xylem and stating that it transports water and mineral salts.

rubric.why: Identifies phloem and its transport function.
rubric.description: Phloem transports prepared food from leaves to other parts of the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming phloem and stating that it transports food.

rubric.why: Gives the main cell components of the compound conducting tissues.
rubric.description: Xylem includes vessels, tracheids, fibres and parenchyma; phloem includes sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres and parenchyma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least two suitable components of xylem or phloem.

modelAnswer: Compound tissues are made of different types of cells that work together to perform a common function.
Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to other parts of the plant; it consists of vessels, tracheids, fibres and parenchyma.
Phloem transports prepared food from leaves to other parts of the plant; it consists of sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres and parenchyma.
